candidates.source_name: 1 Enoch (Ethiopian tradition) / Book of the Watchers (1 Enoch 1-36)
candidates.draft_body:
1 Enoch (Ethiopian tradition) Book of the Watchers (1 Enoch 1-36) (c. 200 BC)

Enoch's vision of Sheol describes four 'hollow places' for the dead awaiting judgment, distinguished by moral status. 'There I saw the spirits of the children of men dead' — including a special place where Abel's soul cries out for vengeance against Cain. This text is one of the most developed pre-Christian Jewish accounts of the intermediate state of the dead, prefiguring the Lukan rich-man-and-Lazarus distinction (Lk 16:19-31). The Tewahedo eschatological tradition draws explicit cross-reference: the intermediate state is real (souls preserve their identity and moral status between bodily death and final resurrection), differentiated (the righteous and wicked are separated), and provisional (awaiting the final judgment).
